title: A template and the things made from it

blocks.md:
## The class is the cutter, the instance is the biscuit

A `class` statement describes a kind of thing: what its instances will be called, what they will know, and what they will do. It is a template, and on its own it holds no station readings. Calling the class — `Sensor()` — builds one instance from that template and hands it back.

The two get confused because the class name appears in both places. `Sensor` is the template; `Sensor()` is a new object. Every call builds a fresh one, so two calls give you two objects that are equal-looking but separate — `first is second` is `False`, and attributes set on one are invisible to the other.

```python
class Sensor:
    pass


a = Sensor()
b = Sensor()
print(type(a).__name__)   # Sensor — the class this instance came from
print(a is b)             # False — two calls, two objects
```

A common mistake is building one instance and binding a second name to it, which looks like two sensors until you change one and both change. The exercise wants two genuinely separate instances: print the class name of the first and whether the two names point at the same object, so the answer has to be `Sensor False`.

blocks.promptMd: `class Sensor: pass`, then `a = Sensor()` and `b = Sensor()`. Is `a is b` true?

choices.md: Yes — they came from the same class, so they are the same object
No — each call built a separate object

blocks.explainMd: Calling a class runs the construction machinery and hands back a brand-new object every time, so `a` and `b` are two distinct instances of one class. `is` asks about object identity, and identity is per instance — the shared class does not make them shared.

blocks.promptMd: What does the class itself hold?

choices.md: The template — the names and behaviour every instance will have
The state of the one object you built from it
A copy of each instance, so it can list them later

blocks.explainMd: The class is a description; the per-thing values live on the instances. Python does not keep a registry of the objects you built, so if you need to know about all your sensors, something in your own code has to collect them in a list.

blocks.promptMd: > Build **two separate** `Sensor` instances, `first` and `second`. Print `type(first).__name__` and whether the two names point at the same object, separated by a space. Output should be `Sensor False`.

hintLadder.md: Look at how `second` is bound in the starter. Is a second object ever built?
Each `Sensor()` call builds one instance, so two separate instances need the class called twice.
Compare with lists: `b = a` gives one list under two names, while `b = list(a)` gives a genuinely second list.

class Sensor:
    pass


first = Sensor()
second = Sensor()

print(type(first).__name__, first is second)

description: A class is the shape. An instance is one of the things.
